Geographic differences in unemployment definitionsPosted on November 16, 2026

SHARE THIS PAGE:

Link Copied

The takeaway
There are six definitions of unemployment, with some constants and some variations, including regional differences.
The question
In a previous FRED Blog post, we discussed the many definitions for unemployment, U-1 through U-6. U-3 is the "official," widely reported number. In this post, we revisit the topic by looking at regional variations for unemployment and how the picture across the country varies as one switches from one definition to another. If you like spotting differences between seemingly identical images, this post is especially for you.
U-1: Unemployed 15 weeks and over
Our first FRED map, above, looks at the long-term unemployed. That is, persons likely having the most in trouble in the labor market. Darker shading indicates higher long-term unemployment rates. To summarize: This unemployment is rate is lower in the Mountain region, about average in the South, and higher elsewhere.
U-2: Unemployed job losers

Our second FRED map, above, looks at those who are unemployed because they lost a job. Typically, persons that may have the most difficulty finding a new job. Persons who quit a job or are in the labor market for the first time but still unemployed usually have better prospects. This map looks similar to the previous one, with a few differences: The middle of the country (Minnesota, Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas) is a bit worse off; the Atlantic coast is a bit better off.
U-3: Headline unemployment

Our third FRED map, above, shows the unemployment rate that is most familiar and most frequently used by the media and policymakers. The South-Central states have high rates, and the Northeast is looking better off here than in the two previous maps. Michigan now stands out.
U-4: Unemployed and discouraged workers

Our fourth FRED map, above, adds discouraged workers. Technically, they don't count as unemployed in U-3 because they're not actively looking for work because they think it's not worth the trouble. This map is almost identical to the previous one, but a perceptive eye will notice three differences: Arizona, Oklahoma, and Massachusetts.
U-5: U-4 plus marginally attached workers

Our fifth FRED map, above, adds yet another group to the previous map: those who could eventually work, if given the opportunity. There are quite a few changes here, with Hawaii and Illinois as particularly affected under this definition.
U-6: U-5 plus reluctant part-timers

Our sixth and final FRED map, above, adds those who work part-time but would prefer to work full-time. This definition is likely the one that shows the biggest visual change in the map, as high rates are now concentrated in the West and a few other states. Compare the first and the last maps:

Only 5 locations are in the highest/darkest category in both those maps: California, Connecticut, Oregon, Washington, and Washington DC.
Only 7 locations are in lowest/lightest category in both those maps: the Dakotas, Missouri, Nebraska, New Hampshire, Vermont, and Wyoming.

How these maps were created: The process is similar for each map. Search FRED for the relevant statistic in a particular state. Then click on the "View map" button.
Suggested by Christian Zimmermann.
